title: Trolling in the Hogan RV, the war over wind blows hot, COVID sidelines Alsobrooks, in notes
summary: Larry Hogan doesn't have to be at MACo to make noise, Angela Alsobrooks comes down with COVID-19, and in the world of renewable energy, is there way to tap the heat coming off the fight over offshore wind?
content:
by Bryan P. Sears, Danielle J. Brown and Christine Condon, Maryland Matters August 15, 2025

by Bryan P. Sears, Danielle J. Brown and Christine Condon, Maryland Matters August 15, 2025

What would it take to get you to drive away with Larry Hogan’s recreational vehicle today, friend?

The answer might have less to do with the finances and floormats of any potential deal and more to do with the political intentions of the two-term former governor.

While speculation abounds over Hogan’s future and a possible run for a third term, the Republican former executive showed this week that he has not lost his knack for trolling.

In a Facebook post Thursday, Hogan posted pictures of the vehicle — with and without the vinyl wrapping that included his campaign logo and stylized Maryland flag — that he used during his failed U.S. Senate bid last year.

“Slightly used 2024 RV, only 15,000 all Maryland miles. Never slept in. Could make a good deal. Or … I guess we could always rewrap it and get back out on the road again?” he teased.

The post did not include a price.

It’s worth noting that Hogan’s post came hours before Gov. Wes Moore (D) was to host a campaign fundraiser in Ocean City.

In the ongoing war over wind farms off the coast of Maryland, the Ocean City Convention Center is apparently a demilitarized zone.

Visitors headed to the second day of the Maryland Association of Counties meeting Thursday morning were greeted by opponents to the wind farm carrying signs and waving to cars on Coastal Highway, and a message on the convention center’s electronic sign that read, “Save the Ocean, Stop the Turbines.”

By the end of the day, both were gone — after complaints from pro-wind groups.

MACo officials confirmed Thursday that they asked that the signs be removed and protesters relocated offsite. Virginia White, MACo’s deputy director, said the protesters obliged, and moved in front of a neighboring business.

She said MACo was aiming to keep the convention center neutral ground. Both sides have booths on the convention floor, she noted.

In a statement, Jen Brock of the pro-wind Oceantic Network said she asked MACo offials to remove the “prominent anti-offshore wind signage” in the interest of neutrality and was grateful they acted “swiftly.”

“The MACo Conference is a neutral space for Marylanders to learn about offshore wind and other key issues shaping Maryland’s counties,” Brock said. “We invite attendees to visit our booth upstairs and learn the facts about offshore wind and the positive impact it is already delivering to local economies here in Maryland.”

A coalition of pro-wind groups, called the Offshore Wind Alliance, paid for billboards on Route 50 and ads in local papers. “Good jobs. Lower utility bills. Less flooding,” reads one of their ads. Meanwhile, some Ocean City businesses hosted anti-wind signs of their own during the conference, which came on the heels of the city’s prominent White Marlin Open billfishing tourney.

Ocean City resident Becky Howe was not initially familiar with MACo, or the slew of politicians it attracts, but volunteered to protest there Thursday because of her passionate opposition to the wind farm. She said it’s a “big lie” that wind farms are environmentally friendly, citing concerns about placing metal structures in the ocean floor, the potential for habitat contamination and harm to wildlife.

“We don’t want them. We told our government we don’t want them. We are demanding that our state representatives listen to us,” Howe said Thursday.

But Rebecca Rehr, director of climate policy and justice at the Maryland League of Conservation Voters, a member of the Offshore Wind Alliance, said she found listening ears on the convention floor. “Almost every person who stopped by our booth while I was staffing it today thanked us for being here and were glad to see the level of support,” Rehr said in a statement.

Her group is pushing for the turbines for economic as well as environmental benefits, she said. “Energy demand is increasing and our electricity bills are rising even faster. With offshore wind, there’s an opportunity to build a clean energy economy that creates jobs and lowers energy bills across the state,” Rehr said.

MACo officials may have stopped the wind wars outside the convention center — but there was no stopping Ocean City Mayor Rick Meehan, a strident wind farm opponent, inside the hall Thursday.

Meehan, in remarks opening the 2026 Maryland Association of Counties summer conference, declared the fight over the wind farm a “David and Goliath battle,” for the future of the resort town.

“Everything we do in Ocean City … is dependent upon our natural resources,” Meehan told the gathering of county officials. “Those include our beautiful sunrise, our natural ecosystem, our recreational fishing, and our commercial fishing. These are all part of the fabric of Ocean City. This is what people live here to enjoy and come here to enjoy when they visit.”

But Meehan sees an existential threat on the horizon: US Wind wants to build what would be the first wind farm off the coast of Maryland. He did not mention the company by name, but said the project would cause irreparable damage.

“Our future and all of these great attributes are being threatened by an outside entity, that will industrialize our sun rise, put a halt to our commercial fishing, damage our ecosystem, and change Ocean City forever — destroy what millions of people, including all of you, enjoy each and every year,” Meehan said.

Signs of the fight — billboards, electronic message boards, and placards — are common throughout the resort town. Meehan said city leaders are building a coalition of leaders in Maryland and Delaware, as well as citizen groups and condominium associations “to fight what could destroy what we enjoy today and our future, for future generations.”

“And it’s a battle. It’s a David-and-Goliath type of battle,” a passionate Meehan told the MACo audience. “But what I can tell you is David won, and our goal is to protect our future, protect Ocean City, and continue to be an economic generator for the town, for the state of Maryland. And I hope we have your support to do that.”

U.S. Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.) was scheduled to attend several MACo events Thursday and Friday — meeting with higher education officials, participating in an Eastern Shore townhall and hosting a fireside chat with fellow Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.).

Those plans fell by the wayside due to Alsobrooks testing positive for COVID-19 Thursday morning, according to a midday notification from her communications team.

“Out of an abundance of caution, she will not be attending the events at Chesapeake College today or the Maryland Association of Counties (MACo) conference in Ocean City on Friday,” said a statement from her office.

While she won’t be attending in person, Alsobrooks said in social media posts that she will “continue to work remotely to serve the people of Maryland.”
